title: Nataraja explained
hook: a dancing Shiva stands at a physics lab in Switzerland, and the place to start reading him is the one part that isn't moving

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the Shiva Purana with Ardhanarishvara, half Shiva and half the goddess, joined like a word and its meaning. Which pair did you thank? Now Shiva begins to dance. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-five.

Physicists walking to work at CERN, the particle physics laboratory near Geneva, pass a statue of Shiva dancing, a gift from India. Engineers, students, visitors with lanyards, coffee in hand. Some of them stop. A god with four arms, one leg kicked high, hair flying out in streams, a ring of fire all around him, one foot pressing down on a small figure lying on its belly. It's a lot to take in on the way to the office. Over the coming days we'll read him piece by piece. Today, where to start looking.
screen: `A DANCING SHIVA AT A PHYSICS LAB.` → `ARMS, FIRE, A RAISED LEG.` → `WHERE TO START LOOKING.`

segments.voice: First the name. Nata means dancer, raja means king. Nataraja is the king of dancers, Shiva as the lord of the dance. In the Tamil country of South India, bronze casters made images like this to be carried in temple processions. Now the inventory, quickly, because we'll take each piece in turn. A small drum in one upper hand. A flame in the other. A lower hand raised, palm out. Another lower hand swung across the body, pointing down at the lifted foot. One foot planted on a small figure. Hair flying out to the sides. A ring of fire framing it all. Each of those will get its own day. But the first thing worth seeing isn't on that list. It's the face. Everything in this image is in motion. The arms swing. The hair streams out sideways, as if he's spinning fast. The leg is kicked across. The flames flicker around the edge. And in the middle of all that motion, the face is calm. Not straining, not grinning with effort. Still. Some images even give it the faintest smile. That's the key to reading the rest. The dance is often called the ananda tandava, the dance of bliss. Whatever this dance is doing, and it's doing a great deal, the dancer isn't frantic about it. The center is quiet. That's a useful thing to take off the pedestal and into an ordinary day. A kitchen at dinner time. A shift with three people out sick. A child melting down in the grocery store. Arms going everywhere. The picture suggests a face that doesn't have to follow the arms.
screen: `NATA, DANCER; RAJA, KING.` · `DRUM, FLAME, HANDS, FOOT, FIRE.` · `EVERYTHING MOVES BUT THE FACE.` · `THE DANCE OF BLISS.` · then, large: `A QUIET CENTER IN THE MOTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a still face. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring your attention to your face. Let the forehead go smooth. Let the jaw drop a little, the tongue rest, the eyes soften. Now let the breath move as it likes, in and out, the belly rising and falling. The body can keep moving with the breath. The face stays quiet. If thoughts start spinning, let them spin like the dancer's hair, out at the edges, while the face stays still in the middle. If you pray, you can say Shiva's name, or the name of God you use, behind that quiet face. The bell holds the time.
Nataraja explained. Nataraja is the king of dancers, Shiva as lord of the dance, and the place to start reading him is the calm face at the center.
Your line: Nataraja explained. Today, in the busiest moment you have, let your hands keep moving and let your face go quiet. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Images of Shiva as Nataraja, the lord of the dance, stand in many Shiva temples, especially in Tamil Nadu, where bronze Natarajas are bathed, dressed and carried out in festival processions.

original.note: Sanskrit: Nataraja, from nata (dancer) and raja (king): the king of dancers.

notes: First of seven Nataraja days (1125–1131). Plan: 1125 the face and inventory; 1126 the drum; 1127 the flame (week end); 1128 the pointing hand and lifted foot; 1129 Apasmara; 1130 the ring of fire and the hair; 1131 Chidambaram. The raised abhaya palm was taught on day 1037 and is only mentioned here.
CERN statue: a Nataraja statue presented by India stands at CERN. The year of the gift was deliberately left out. Confirm the description.

Nata/raja gloss is the standard reading of the compound. 'Ananda tandava' as the name of this dance is a common identification; some traditions distinguish several dances of Shiva. Confirm framing ('often called').
'Bronze casters made them to be carried in temple processions' is a general statement about South Indian festival bronzes; period names left out.
